title: Building a Multi-Step Approval Workflow in Zoho Creator
heading: Building a Multi-Step Approval Workflow in Zoho Creator
excerpt: How to architect a document approval system with role-based access, email notifications, and dynamic form sections - all inside Zoho Creator without a single line of external code.
body:
One of the most common requests from clients is: "We need an approval workflow that routes requests through multiple managers before anything gets processed." Zoho Creator handles this entirely within its low-code environment.

The Architecture

A multi-step approval workflow in Creator typically involves three layers: the submission form, a workflow trigger, and status-gated record views for each approver role. The key insight is treating approval stages as a field value, not as separate records. Each stage change fires a notification, and the next approver's view is gated by that stage value.

Role-Based Page Access

Creator's built-in permission system lets you gate entire pages by user role. Roles like Line Manager, HR Head, and Finance Lead are defined in the app's Access section. Conditional visibility on report columns ensures each role only sees records in their stage, keeping the interface clean and preventing confusion between approvers.

Dynamic Form Sections

The approval form uses Deluge field actions to reveal the approval comment box only when the record is in the correct stage for that user. This prevents premature approvals and enforces the workflow order. Attempting to approve out of sequence simply shows a read-only view with no action buttons.

Notification Chaining

Each approval stage triggers a notification to the next approver, passing the record ID in a deep link directly to the Creator portal record. Using the zoho.appuri function in Deluge, you can construct a direct URL so approvers land exactly on the record they need to action - no hunting through lists required.

  • Stage 1: Line Manager approves, status advances to Pending HR
  • Stage 2: HR Head approves, status advances to Pending Finance
  • Stage 3: Finance Lead approves, final actions trigger

Audit Trail

Creator's built-in record history captures every field change automatically. For compliance-sensitive workflows, this gives you a timestamped log of who approved what and when, without any additional development effort.

Why This Pattern Works

The entire workflow lives inside a single Creator app. No Zoho Flow needed, no external webhooks. For businesses in Mauritius looking to digitalise paper-based approval processes, this is often the fastest path from zero to a working system - deployable in days, not weeks.

title: Deluge vs JavaScript: Why Zoho's Scripting Language Is Underrated
heading: Deluge vs JavaScript: Why Zoho's Scripting Language Is Underrated
excerpt: Developers coming from Node.js often dismiss Deluge as limited. Here's why that's wrong, what makes it genuinely powerful, and where it actually falls short.
body:
Every developer I meet who has heard of Deluge has the same reaction: "It looks like a toy language." They are not entirely wrong - but they are missing what makes it brilliant for its context.

What Deluge Actually Is

Deluge (Data Enriched Language for the Universal Grid Environment) is Zoho's proprietary scripting language. It runs server-side inside Zoho's platform - in Creator workflows, CRM functions, Books automations, and more. Think of it as a scripting layer tightly coupled to Zoho's data layer, not a general-purpose language.

Where Deluge Wins

The killer feature is native Zoho integration. Calling another Zoho app in Deluge takes three lines: fetch the record, read the field, done. In JavaScript, the equivalent involves OAuth token management, API versioning, error handling boilerplate, and often a full SDK import. In Deluge, authentication and rate limit handling are provided by the platform - that context is simply free.

Map and List Manipulation

Deluge has surprisingly capable collection types. Maps (key-value stores) and Lists work intuitively for building API payloads, transforming records, and iterating over datasets. For the kind of business logic that lives inside Zoho - computing totals, building notification messages, transforming incoming webhook data - Deluge handles it cleanly.

Where Deluge Falls Short

No npm ecosystem. No async/await. No closures. String manipulation is verbose. Complex JSON parsing requires careful nesting of get() calls. For anything compute-heavy or requiring external libraries, you would reach for Catalyst Functions (which run Node.js or Java) instead.

The Right Mental Model

Stop comparing Deluge to JavaScript. Compare it to SQL stored procedures or AWS Lambda with automatic IAM. It is a constrained, opinionated scripting environment that optimises for one thing: manipulating Zoho data with zero infrastructure overhead. In that context, it is remarkably effective.

  • Use Deluge for: CRM hooks, Creator workflows, Books automation, intra-Zoho data sync
  • Use Catalyst Functions for: heavy computation, external library needs, complex APIs
  • Use Zoho Flow for: multi-app orchestration with conditional logic and retries

title: Deluge Tips Most Developers Don't Know About
heading: Deluge Tips Most Developers Don't Know About
excerpt: After months of daily Deluge scripting, here are the lesser-known behaviours and patterns that significantly changed how I write business logic in Zoho.
body:
Deluge documentation covers the basics well. But after months of daily scripting, you encounter behaviours and patterns that are not obvious from the docs. Here are the ones that changed how I write business logic.

The delay() Function Is Not What You Think

Most developers assume delay() in Deluge works like setTimeout() in JavaScript - pause execution for a moment, then continue. It does not. The delay() function in Deluge is specifically designed for use inside Zoho Flow functions, not standalone Creator or CRM Deluge scripts. Using it incorrectly causes silent failures that are notoriously hard to debug because no error is thrown - execution simply stops.

If you need to pace API calls or add a wait inside Creator, the correct approach is to use scheduled functions with state stored in a record field, not to attempt delays inline. Understanding this single distinction will save hours of debugging.

toJSONList() vs toList() - They Are Not Interchangeable

When you receive JSON from an external API, Deluge parses the response as a string. Calling toJSONList() converts a JSON array string into an iterable Deluge List of Maps. Calling toList() instead gives you a list of raw strings, meaning your subsequent .get() calls on each item will silently fail. This is one of the most common sources of empty values in Deluge functions that call external APIs.

getUrl() Silently Strips Headers in Some Contexts

When using invokeurl with custom headers, Creator's sandbox environment strips certain auth headers during testing but passes them through in production. This means a function that appears to fail in the Creator IDE may work correctly once deployed. Always test Deluge functions that hit external APIs against the actual production endpoint, not only in the sandbox.

Map.put() Overwrites Silently

Calling put() on a Map with an existing key does not warn you - it overwrites. This becomes a problem in loops where you are building a map of results and accidentally use the same key twice. Always check your key generation logic when iterating and building maps. A duplicated key in a loop is one of the hardest bugs to spot in Deluge.

The input Object Behaves Differently Based on Context

In Creator, input refers to the triggering record in on-submit and on-validate contexts. In scheduled functions, there is no input object at all. In CRM custom functions, input is passed explicitly from the trigger. Treating these as equivalent leads to null reference errors that look identical but have different root causes. Always confirm which context your function runs in before relying on input.

The most dangerous Deluge bugs are the ones that fail silently. No exception is thrown, no log entry is written, and the function simply exits without completing. Always verify your critical write operations actually executed by logging the return value of the operation.

Using zoho.loginuserid vs zoho.adminuserid

zoho.loginuserid returns the user currently executing the function. In scheduled functions, this returns the app admin's email. In user-triggered workflows, it returns the logged-in user. Confusing these two in notification logic means your scheduled tasks send emails from the wrong address context, or your notifications attribute actions to the wrong person. Know which one you need before wiring up any notification system.

title: Zoho Flow vs Deluge: Choosing the Right Automation Tool
heading: Zoho Flow vs Deluge: Choosing the Right Automation Tool
excerpt: Both can automate Zoho workflows, but they solve different problems. Here's a framework for deciding which to reach for - and when you need both.
body:
This is the question I get asked most often by clients and fellow developers: "Should I use Flow or write a Deluge function?" The answer is contextual - here is the framework I use.

The Fundamental Difference

Deluge runs synchronously inside a Zoho app. It is tightly coupled to a specific event (form submission, button click, record update) within Creator, CRM, or Books. It executes in the same session and has direct access to the triggering record's data.

Zoho Flow is an integration platform that runs asynchronously and independently. It listens for triggers across apps and orchestrates actions across the entire Zoho suite - and beyond it, connecting to 900+ third-party services.

Use Deluge When...

  • Logic is tightly coupled to a single app's data model
  • You need synchronous execution (show/hide fields, compute values on the fly)
  • Performance matters - Deluge runs in milliseconds, Flow has execution latency
  • The automation stays entirely within one Zoho app

Use Zoho Flow When...

  • You need to connect two or more Zoho apps - or external services
  • You want visual debugging, execution logs, and retry logic out of the box
  • Non-developers need to modify the automation logic
  • You are integrating with tools like Slack, Google Workspace, or third-party ERPs

The Hybrid Pattern

The most powerful setups use both. A Deluge function handles the complex data processing and calculation within Creator, then calls a Flow webhook to trigger downstream orchestration - syncing data to CRM, sending a Slack notification, and creating a Books invoice, all in parallel. Deluge does the precision work; Flow manages the logistics.

A Note on Debugging

Flow's execution history is one of its strongest features in practice. When something goes wrong in a multi-app pipeline, Flow shows you exactly which step failed, what payload it received, and what it returned. Deluge gives you nothing unless you explicitly log to a record. For complex cross-app workflows, this visibility alone often justifies using Flow even when Deluge could technically do the job.

title: Getting Started with Zoho Catalyst 2.0: Serverless for the Zoho Ecosystem
heading: Getting Started with Zoho Catalyst 2.0
excerpt: Catalyst 2.0 evolved from a simple serverless platform into a full cloud development environment. Here's what that means for Zoho developers, and how to think about it.
body:
Catalyst started as Zoho's answer to AWS Lambda - a serverless platform for running functions without managing infrastructure. Version 2.0 expanded it into a full cloud development environment with datastores, caches, queues, AI/ML services, and DevOps tooling. For Zoho developers, it is the escape hatch for anything Deluge cannot do.

When Do You Need Catalyst?

You reach for Catalyst when you need to:

  • Use npm packages or Java libraries not available in Deluge
  • Build a standalone web application backed by Zoho data
  • Run compute-heavy processing such as PDF generation, image manipulation, or ML inference
  • Implement a custom REST API consumed by external systems
  • Process async event queues at scale

The Core Primitives

Catalyst 2.0 gives you several building blocks that work together. Functions are your serverless compute layer, running Node.js or Java code on demand or on a schedule. The Datastore is a managed relational database accessible via a REST API or the Catalyst SDK. Cache is a Redis-compatible key-value store ideal for tokens, rate-limited API responses, and configuration. Queues let you decouple processing from user-facing workflows, essential for high-volume operations.

Catalyst Datastore vs Zoho Creator Reports

A question that comes up often: why use Catalyst Datastore when Creator already stores data? The Datastore is appropriate when you need high-volume inserts, complex SQL joins across large datasets, or data that is owned by your serverless backend rather than a Creator app. If the data naturally belongs to a Creator form and is accessed through Creator pages, keep it in Creator. If you are building an independent service that happens to connect to Zoho, the Datastore is the right layer.

Connecting Back to Zoho Apps

Catalyst functions can call any Zoho API using the Catalyst SDK's built-in connector. This handles OAuth authentication automatically within the Zoho ecosystem, so you do not manage tokens manually when calling Zoho CRM, Books, or Creator APIs from your functions.

The Bigger Picture

Catalyst 2.0 positions Zoho developers to build production-grade cloud applications - not just automations. Combined with Creator for the front-end and Deluge for in-app logic, Catalyst fills the pro-code layer that previously required stepping outside the Zoho ecosystem entirely. For developers in Mauritius working with Zoho-heavy client stacks, this means you can build end-to-end solutions without leaving the platform.

title: MRA E-Invoicing Compliance with Zoho: A Technical Overview
heading: MRA E-Invoicing Compliance with Zoho: A Technical Overview
excerpt: How the Mauritius Revenue Authority's mandatory e-invoicing framework integrates with the Zoho stack - the architecture, the compliance requirements, and what Zoho developers need to understand.
body:
The Mauritius Revenue Authority's e-invoicing mandate is no longer optional. As a developer at MetaBox Technology - a certified EBS (Electronic Billing System) provider - I have been directly involved in building compliant invoicing integrations for local businesses. Here is what Zoho developers need to understand.

What MRA E-Invoicing Requires

The MRA framework requires businesses to transmit invoice data to MRA's API in real-time at the point of sale. Each invoice must include a cryptographic QR code, a unique fiscal receipt number, and a verifiable digital signature. Non-compliance carries significant penalties, and the mandate covers virtually all VAT-registered businesses in Mauritius.

Where Zoho Fits

Most local SMEs either bill through Zoho Books or through a custom Creator application. In both cases, the integration point is Zoho's Deluge scripting layer: a function that fires on invoice creation, packages the invoice data according to MRA specifications, transmits it to the MRA API, and writes the returned fiscal receipt number and QR code data back into the invoice record before the PDF is generated.

The Architecture at a Glance

  • Invoice created in Zoho Books or a custom Creator app
  • On-save Deluge function fires and packages the invoice payload in MRA-compliant format
  • Authenticated API call to the MRA endpoint transmits the data in real-time
  • MRA returns a fiscal receipt number and QR code payload
  • Deluge writes both values back to the invoice record
  • Invoice PDF is generated with the QR code embedded, ready to issue

Token Management Considerations

MRA API tokens are time-limited and need refreshing. Handling token refresh inside the same Deluge function that processes each invoice creates unnecessary latency and a single point of failure. A cleaner architecture separates token management into a scheduled Catalyst function that refreshes credentials on a timer and stores the current token in Catalyst Cache. The invoice-processing Deluge function reads the token from cache, keeping the transactional path fast and decoupled from auth concerns.

Why This Matters for the Mauritius Developer Community

Zoho has 33% annual growth in Mauritius and recently opened its first regional office at Ebene Cybercity. Most local businesses run on Zoho. MRA e-invoicing compliance is mandatory. A Zoho developer who understands both the platform internals and the local regulatory landscape is in a rare and genuinely valuable position - the intersection of technical depth and local context is where real opportunity lies.

title: Building a Custom Zoho Books Extension for MNS Tax Return Filing
heading: Building a Custom Zoho Books Extension for MNS Tax Return Filing
excerpt: Zoho Books handles VAT well, but filing returns in the MRA's MNS format requires a custom extension. Here's the architecture for building one that exports correctly structured tax data.
body:
Zoho Books handles VAT accounting correctly for Mauritius, but when it comes to preparing returns in the MRA's specific MNS (Monthly/Quarterly Nil Statement) format, there is no out-of-the-box export. This is exactly the kind of gap a custom Zoho Books extension is designed to fill.

What a Zoho Books Extension Is

A Zoho Books extension is a package that adds custom functionality to Books - new tabs, buttons, sidebar widgets, and Deluge-backed actions - without modifying the core application. Extensions are deployed through the Zoho Marketplace or as private extensions for a specific organisation. They run inside the Books context, with access to Books data through the Zoho Finance APIs and Deluge's native Books integration functions.

Understanding the MNS Format

The MRA's MNS format for VAT returns requires output data organised by tax period, broken down by standard-rated supplies, zero-rated supplies, exempt supplies, and input tax credits. Each line item must reference the original invoice or purchase record. The format is structured and specific - it cannot be approximated by a generic Books report export.

The Extension Architecture

The extension adds a dedicated "Tax Returns" tab inside the Books interface. A Deluge function fetches all invoices and bills for the selected tax period using the Zoho Books API. It then categorises each transaction by VAT treatment, aggregates the totals per MNS field definition, and generates a downloadable file in the correct format. The user selects the period, clicks Generate, and receives a ready-to-submit file without leaving Books.

  • Custom tab added to Books navigation via the extension manifest
  • Period selector widget lets the user define the tax quarter
  • Deluge function queries Books API for all transactions in range
  • Classification logic maps each transaction to its MNS field
  • Output file generated client-side and downloaded directly

Handling Edge Cases

The classification logic is where most of the complexity lives. Credit notes must offset the original supply. Transactions that span VAT periods due to payment date vs invoice date differences need specific handling. Purchases from non-VAT-registered suppliers must be excluded from input tax claims. Building this logic in Deluge requires careful reading of MRA's technical specification, and testing against real historical data before any production deployment.

Why This Is a Niche Worth Owning

This type of localisation work sits at the intersection of Zoho technical knowledge and Mauritius regulatory understanding. Very few developers hold both. An extension like this, once built and validated, is reusable across every VAT-registered business on Zoho Books in Mauritius - and that is a significant and growing market.

title: Using Zoho Catalyst Cache to Speed Up Deluge API Calls
heading: Using Zoho Catalyst Cache to Speed Up Deluge API Calls
excerpt: Deluge functions that hit external APIs on every execution are slow and rate-limit-prone. Here is how to use Catalyst's managed cache layer to solve that.
body:
A common performance problem in Zoho implementations: a Deluge function that calls an external API on every single record save. At low volume, no problem. At scale, you hit rate limits and slow response times fast.

The Pattern

Catalyst's Cache segment is a managed Redis-compatible key-value store accessible from both Catalyst Functions and, via the Catalyst SDK, from Deluge. The strategy is straightforward: cache slow or rate-limited data at the Catalyst layer, refresh it on a scheduled basis, and let every Deluge call read from cache instead of hitting the external API directly.

How It Works in Practice

A Catalyst scheduled function runs every 30 minutes. It fetches the data that would otherwise be requested on every Deluge call - exchange rates, OAuth tokens, product price lists, tax rate tables, or any configuration data. That data is stored in Catalyst Cache with a TTL slightly longer than the refresh interval, ensuring there is always a valid value available. Each Deluge function then reads from cache in under 10 milliseconds instead of making a live API call that might take 800ms or trigger a rate limit error.

What This Solves

Instead of hitting an external API thousands of times per day, the external call happens once every 30 minutes. Rate limits disappear. Response times drop from hundreds of milliseconds to single digits. The Deluge function itself becomes more reliable because it no longer depends on an external service being available at the exact moment of execution.

Where to Apply This

This pattern is applicable to any data that is expensive to fetch but does not change on every request: OAuth tokens, currency exchange rates, product price lists, postal code lookups, tax rate tables, and application configuration values. If your Deluge function is fetching the same data on every execution, it almost certainly belongs in Catalyst Cache.
